title: A Sleepless Night and a Great Reversal
summary: The king cannot sleep, has the royal chronicles read to him, and learns that Mordecai once saved his life and was never rewarded. At that moment Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's execution, and the king asks him how to honor a man the king delights in. Haman, assuming he is the man, describes a royal parade, and is ordered to give that honor to Mordecai; his wife and advisers then foretell his fall.
story: At the end of chapter 5 Haman went to bed pleased, with a gallows standing in his courtyard and an invitation to the queen's second banquet. Esther's request is still unspoken. This chapter happens in the single night and morning between the two banquets, and it turns the book around. The plot against the king recorded back in 2:21-23, when Mordecai exposed two eunuchs and the matter was written in the chronicles, suddenly returns. Nothing in this chapter is a miracle, yet everything arrives exactly on time, and the reversal of Haman and Mordecai that will be completed in chapters 7 to 9 begins here in miniature.
historical:
Persian kings kept official records, and the book refers to them several times (2:23; 6:1; 10:2). The Book of Records mentioned here would have noted matters of state, including service done to the king. Greek historians describe the Persian custom of rewarding royal benefactors; Herodotus reports that men who did the king a service were recorded and honored, and names such benefactors in his account of Xerxes' war with Greece. That Mordecai's deed went unrewarded for about five years (from the king's seventh year to his twelfth) would have been a failure of royal honor that a king was bound to correct.

The danger of conspiracy was not theoretical. Xerxes himself was assassinated in 465 BC in a palace plot involving his own court officials. A story in which eunuchs guarding the king's door plan to kill him fits the real hazards of the Persian palace.
cultural:
Honor in the ancient world was public. To be honored was to be seen being honored. Haman's proposal draws on the most visible signs of royal favor: a robe the king himself had worn, a horse the king had ridden with a royal crest on its head, and a high official leading the man through the city square proclaiming his honor. Wearing the king's own garment symbolized sharing in his dignity, which is why such a request was dangerous; Haman asks for something very close to the king's own person. In a similar way, Joseph was dressed in fine garments and paraded in the king's second chariot in Egypt (Genesis 41:42-43).

Haman's going home with his head covered shows grief and shame, the same gesture David's people made in mourning (2 Samuel 15:30). His advisers' reply, that he cannot prevail against Mordecai because Mordecai is Jewish, reflects the ancient assumption that peoples had their own destinies and that a people's fortune could be read in events.
literary: This is the book's central chapter and the pivot of its structure of reversals. The storytelling is comic and precise. The narrator lets the reader hear Haman's private thought (verse 6), so that his long, eager description of the honors he expects to receive becomes painful to watch. The key phrase, the man whom the king is delighted to honor, is repeated again and again, and it ends in Haman's own mouth as he proclaims it before Mordecai. Many scholars see the book arranged around this turning point, with events before it mirrored by events after it: two banquets of Esther, two edicts, Haman's rise and fall, Mordecai's humiliation in sackcloth and his exaltation in royal garments. The chapter closes with the king's eunuchs hurrying Haman to the banquet, leaving no time for him to recover.

outline.t: The sleepless king reads of Mordecai's unrewarded service
Haman arrives in the outer court
Haman proposes honors he thinks are for himself
Haman leads Mordecai through the city square
Haman's shame and his advisers' warning

doctrines.note: A king's insomnia, a chance reading from the right page of the chronicles, and Haman's early arrival combine to reverse the story. The chapter is the book's clearest picture of providence: God governing events through ordinary causes without breaking in visibly.

Haman's advisers, not Israelite prophets, recognize that his downfall has begun and cannot be stopped. The chapter implies that the fate of God's people rests in a power beyond Persian law and Haman's ambitions.
Haman's humiliation is the first stage of a just reversal. He comes to ask for Mordecai's death and leaves having honored him, an example of the biblical pattern that the proud are brought low.

words.note: Nadad, to flee or wander. The Hebrew says literally that the king's sleep fled. The verb is often used of fugitives or wandering birds. The book gives no reason for the sleeplessness, and the omission invites the reader to ask who is behind it.

Yeqar, honor, preciousness, esteem. The word is fairly rare in the Hebrew Bible and appears more often in Esther than anywhere else. It dominates the chapter: the king asks what honor Mordecai received, and the phrase about the man the king delights to honor is built on it.

Chaphets, to delight in, to take pleasure in. The repeated phrase the man whom the king delights to honor uses this verb. Haman is sure he is the one the king delights in; the king's delight turns out to rest on the man Haman hates.

Naphal, to fall. Haman's advisers use the word twice in verse 13: his fall has begun, and he will surely fall before Mordecai. The word recurs in chapter 7, when Haman literally falls on Esther's couch, and the narrator lets it carry both meanings.

christ: The chapter's reversal, in which the humbled man is exalted and the proud man is compelled to proclaim his honor, fits a pattern that runs through Scripture and reaches its height in Christ. It is a thematic connection, not a prophecy. Paul writes that Jesus “humbled Himself and became obedient to death— even death on a cross,” and that “God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names” (Philippians 2:8-9). Mordecai's reward comes from a human king who had forgotten him; the New Testament speaks of a God who forgets no act of faithfulness. The advisers' sense that no one can prevail against Mordecai's people also echoes the Bible's conviction that God preserves the people through whom he will bring blessing to the world.

hard.q: Is this chapter describing God's hand, or just a string of lucky coincidences?
hard.a: The text never says that God kept the king awake or guided the reading. A reader who does not believe in providence can read it as a well-crafted story of coincidence, and some modern scholars read the book mainly as a court tale about human wit and fortune. But the density of coincidence is the point of the chapter: the sleepless night, the passage read, the unrewarded deed, and Haman's early arrival all converge within hours of Mordecai's intended execution. Jewish and Christian readers have long taken this concentration of timing as the book's way of pointing to God without naming him, and Haman's own advisers sense that something larger than chance is at work. The book leaves the reader to draw that conclusion rather than stating it, which is itself a reflection of how providence is usually experienced: seen clearly only in hindsight.

questions: Mordecai's good deed went unrewarded for years before it mattered. How do you respond when faithfulness seems forgotten?
Haman assumes the honor must be for him. Where does self-importance distort the way you hear other people's words?
Looking back, can you name a time when ordinary events came together in a way you later saw as more than coincidence?
